articles.title: Xi-Putin-Trump summit was heavy on symbolism, light on substance – and not exactly a Yalta II
paragraphs: It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.
Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.
But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?
As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.
What were the key takeaways from the meeting?

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi . Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.
And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.
In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls . In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985 : “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”

All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.
The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.

There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.
Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.
Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.
Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.

What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.

articles.title: Breaking the silence: Pratishta’s journey from childhood abuse to advocacy
paragraphs: Editorial note: This article contains mention of gender-based violence, sexual assault, violence against children, and child sexual abuse, which may be triggering for some readers.

November 25 to December 10, 2026, marks the UN’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence . However, even as gender-based violence gets more recognition globally, survivors are still struggling to access social or legal justice. South Asia is no exception to this. Global Voices sat down with one survivor of childhood abuse who uses her experience to fuel her advocacy work today.

South Asia is home to nearly one quarter of the world’s population, woven with a diverse, culture-driven fabric where women are often celebrated as goddesses. However, this veneration doesn’t necessarily mean South Asian women are safe or free from abuse.

In Nepal, there are far too many examples of crimes against women and girls. For instance, Nirmala Panta, 13, was found dead in a sugarcane field — a case which has remained unsolved since 2018. Bhagirathi Bhatta, 17, was choked to death when returning home from school in 2021, and Inisha BK, 16, was found unconscious in the Janagaran Community Forest in Surkhet in early 2026. A similar yet shocking case is that of a 3-year-old Garima, who was found dead inside an abandoned house in Jeetpur in southern Nepal. While these tragic rape and murder cases leave deep scars in Nepal’s national psyche, even more cases go unheard and unreported.

Sparking a nationwide outrage, such cases force the country to confront a collective shame. They raise questions around human morality, diminishing trust and affection in society, and breakdowns in the legal justice system. In the face of these atrocities, women took to the streets, demanding justice and accountability. But their calls fell on deaf ears.

“I was 11 years old when I was sexually abused by my close maternal uncle for four days,” said Pratishtha Gautam in an online interview with Global Voices in November 2026. Opening up about this incident was a real challenge for her, yet she was committed to sharing her story.

Her childhood was by no means easy. She moved regularly as a child, and at seven years old, she was sent to her maternal uncle’s house for a year because her parents had to move away to address her younger brother’s health issues.
It was in this house that a monster took away her innocence.

After four days of abuse, she escaped on the fifth day with the help of her neighbors. Finally getting a chance to flee from her abuser, she “rushed to my room, quickly happened to lock the door by chance, thankfully, and began to scream out to my neighbors.” She had witnessed men mistreating women in her neighborhood growing up and feels lucky that her cries weren’t met with indifference.

She felt neglected growing up and believed her parents loved her younger brother more. This left her with a sense of detachment from her family. The abuse only compounded her challenges. As she says, “It was not easy at all.”

The experience has left her with scars: “I have been awakened with nightmares since that incident, making my sleep extremely difficult.” She also suffers from panic attacks when she sees material about sexual abuse. She describes feeling like her heart is swollen and being torn apart. When triggered, she often freezes up and dissociates.

According to research from the American Academy of Pediatrics journal, child sexual abuse can be incredibly detrimental to a person’s long-term mental well-being. Child abuse survivors are more likely to suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, eating disorders and disturbances, sleep disruption and insomnia, and dissociation, as well as adverse physical health conditions and attachment issues, according to the Center of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse .

This highlights the immense scale of pain that many children experience when they are victims of sexual abuse. Not everyone is able to speak out about such abuses. This is particularly true in South Asia, where there is a social stigma around abuse, due to entrenched ideas around “purity.”

She resents suggestions that it is women’s responsibility to not “tempt” men or draw attention to themselves. “Why should we be the ones to cover ourselves up?” she asks. She refuses to hide and stay silent while her abuser “is living free somewhere.” She refuses to remain invisible.

Even as many countries make strides in gender equality, gender-based violence continues to be a major issue. In a 2023 report, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly one in three (31.6 percent) of women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime — roughly 840 million women and girls.

At the root of gender-based violence lies a belief in male superiority. Not all men would openly endorse this belief, yet many see themselves as protectors of the women in their lives: their sisters, mothers, girlfriends, and wives. But this notion of protection is deeply flawed, especially when it comes at the cost of women’s freedom, mobility, access to opportunities, dreams, and agency.

Gautam recognizes this notion in her own upbringing. She had dreams of her own and was ready to chase them, but her family had a different plan for her. They wanted “to get me married off,” she said. She kept her independence through stubbornness and determination.

Today, Gautam lives in Adelaide in South Australia. She suffers from complex PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and works as a mental health clinician helping other survivors of abuse. She reflected, in a heavy tone, on being a thousand miles away from home but safe and independent.

PTSD and insomnia aren’t the only consequences of her abuse. While she was once married, she struggled to cope with her trauma, and it negatively impacted her relationship, eventually leading to divorce.

As part of her treatment, Gautam has met regularly with psychotherapists over the years. Eventually, even that wasn’t enough. She put everything on hold for a year and gave herself time and space to focus on her mental health. She believes she would have difficulty living a normal life and still struggles with relationships. “I hate men. I used to hate them and still have trust issues,” she said.

Even as she struggles to process her own trauma, she also works to help others recover from abuse and offers pro bono psychological counseling. Being part of the solution has in some ways helped her heal. Her passion as a mental health clinician goes beyond her own individual experiences to the collective — a reminder to be empathetic as humans first.

articles.title: Independent, Gen Z and Latino voters helped deliver a Democratic wave in 2026 – but that doesn’t mean a lasting realignment
paragraphs: The Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections raises an important question about American politics. Are independent, Gen Z and Latino voters building a new Democratic coalition, or are they sending a warning to both parties that their support cannot be taken for granted?
The preliminary evidence suggests something more complicated.

Our analysis, including a deep dive into the 2026 Voter Poll conducted by the market research firm SSRS, points to three factors behind the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories: a substantial shift among independent voters toward Democratic candidates, stronger Democratic turnout relative to Republicans, and declining enthusiasm among voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024.
Gen Z, who are people born from 1997 to 2012, and Latino voters played important roles in these shifts.

But the results should not automatically be interpreted as a lasting Democratic realignment. These voters may be demonstrating a willingness to reconsider their political choices when governing parties fail to meet their expectations.

The overlapping influence of independent, younger and Latino voters helps explain the scale of the Democratic gains. Our analysis, based on voter poll data, suggests that independents, who made up about one-third of voters, contributed approximately 52% of the Democrats’ national popular vote margin in House races. Latino voters contributed an estimated 23% of that margin, while voters ages 18 to 29 contributed approximately 39%.
Because these groups overlap, their contributions cannot be added together. But the figures illustrate how important each was to the Democratic advantage.
In our book, “ The Independent Voter,” co-authored with Omar Ali, we examine the growing influence of independent voters and their often unpredictable voting behavior.
Independent voters, among the most important contributors to Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to shift between parties.

In 2008, they favored Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama by 8 percentage points. Four years later, they backed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney by 5 points. In the 2016 presidential election, independents favored Republican Trump by 4 points before swinging toward Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, supporting him by 13 points.

In the 2024 presidential election, independents narrowly favored Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump, 49% to 46%. However, Trump performed better among independents in key battleground states, including Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina .
In our research spanning nearly five decades, Dan Hunting and I, Thom Reilly, found that independents exhibit considerably greater volatility in their voting patterns than Democrats and Republicans.

The 3-point advantage independents gave Harris in 2024 provides a useful baseline for understanding their much larger shift toward Democratic candidates in 2026. A November 2026 national survey of more than 90,000 people found that voters identifying with neither major party favored Democratic House candidates by more than 20 percentage points.

Our analysis of voter poll data showed that independents favored House Democrats by 59% to 37%. In addition, independents’ support was consequential in several Republican-held Senate seats that flipped to Democrats, with independent voters providing the margin needed for victory in six of the nine races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina.

The emerging pattern may represent another turn in a longer cycle of electoral volatility among independents. Rather than embracing either party, independent voters appear willing to reconsider their choices as political and economic conditions change.
Did Republicans switch sides or stay home?
There is some disagreement about what produced the midterm Democratic wave.

Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston argue that Republican abstention – those who chose not to vote – was more important nationally than large-scale partisan crossover voting. They report that only approximately 6% of self-identified Republicans voted for Democratic House candidates.
Yet the evidence also demonstrates some crossover voting.
An analysis by the research firm NORC found that approximately 1 in 10 2024 Trump voters in 2026 supported Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina and Texas.
Both dynamics appear to have played a role.

Democrats benefited from stronger participation among their supporters and reduced turnout among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. In several competitive races, Republican defections and strong independent support also contributed to Democratic victories.

Understanding these differences is important. A shift in election results does not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. It may reflect changes in who participates. The 2026 results suggest that both factors were at work.
Gen Z voters were another important part of the Democratic gains.

In 2026, 66% of voters ages 18–29 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 30% who backed Republicans. That 36-point Democratic advantage was substantially larger than the 14-point margin in 2024, according to Tufts University .

There was also evidence of voters switching party choices. Among young people who voted for Trump in 2024 and participated in the 2026 election, 16% supported a Democratic House candidate. And 67% of young voters disapproved of Trump’s performance as president in 2026.
Gallup found that 56% of Gen Z adults identify as political independents, underscoring the weaker ties many younger Americans have to the two major parties.

Combined with economic dissatisfaction and distrust of political institutions, this suggests that younger voters may be especially willing to reconsider their choices when the party in power fails to meet their expectations or deliver on its promises.
Latino voters showed a similar pattern, but with some differences.
More than 6 in 10 Latino voters supported Democratic House candidates in 2026, according to a NORC survey . That reverses much of the Republican gains among these voters in 2024.

There was also evidence of volatility among Latinos. A postelection survey by UnidosUS and BSP Research found that 17% of Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic House candidates in 2026, compared with just 3% of Harris voters who supported Republicans.
Texas offers an example of how these voting groups overlapped.

According to our analysis of the voter poll data, 68% of Latino voters supported Democrat James Talarico, compared with 30% who backed his Republican opponent. Among voters ages 18 to 29, Talarico won 79% to 19%, while independents favored him by 64% to 33%.
Of course, these groups overlap. A voter can be Latino, young and independent, so their contributions cannot simply be added together numerically.
Still, Latinos’ strong support for Talarico illustrates how shifts among these voting groups helped Democrats win in a traditionally Republican state, perhaps shaping a new composite demographic.
The lesson of 2026 may be less about Democratic realignment than about political accountability.
Republicans benefited in 2024 from dissatisfaction with Democratic governance. Two years later, Democrats benefited from dissatisfaction with Republican governance.

articles.title: Growing up displaced in Cameroon after ten years of conflict
paragraphs: For children displaced by Cameroon’s ongoing armed Anglophone conflict, reaching safety has not ended the struggle. In Buea, the capital of Cameroon’s Southwest region, some children are balancing school with market trading to help their families survive.

“At least here in Buea, there are no gunshots, and we do not have to hide in the bush,” says 11-year-old Lorane in an interview with Global Voices, describing the relative safety his family found after fleeing their home in Cameroon’s conflict-affected Southwest Region.

The move brought the children to a calmer environment where they could resume schooling and live with less fear of armed violence. But leaving their communities also meant losing homes, familiar surroundings, friendships and, for some, years of education. In Buea, the struggle to rebuild family livelihoods has introduced another responsibility to their lives: helping their parents earn a living.

The Anglophone crisis in Cameroon began in 2016, when teachers and lawyers began protesting over the perceived marginalization of English-language education and common-law systems, which they say favored French. This escalated into wider demonstrations and a government crackdown. In 2017, the situation deteriorated into armed conflict between government forces and separatist groups seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions as a state commonly referred to as Ambazonia . The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that between 2.1 and 2.2 million people have been displaced due to the violence and insecurity.

At Buea’s OIC Market, children from displaced families sell bleach, puff-puff, plantains, ginger, garlic, and oranges, particularly during weekends and before school. Some travel from neighboring communities to help their parents sell goods, while others work around family-owned stalls.

For 14-year-old Joy, this means traveling from Mutengene to Buea on weekends to sell sachets of bleach. Her mother buys the bleach in bulk and repackages it into smaller sachets, which Joy sells for CFA 100 (about USD 0.17) each. She says daily sales can reach CFA 10,000–15,000 (about USD 16.81–25.21), helping support the household and her siblings.

Joy has been working since her family fled their village when she was in Class Five. “They were shooting guns in my village, so my mum had to bring us here so we could continue school,” she says. She has since become used to the routine, which allows her to contribute to the family while continuing her education.

For 14-year-old Sidoine, displacement meant losing four years of schooling. Her family fled Ekona after their house was burned while they were away at the farm. She remembers hiding in the bushes when they heard attacks were coming, unsure what would happen next. Her family eventually left their hometown, Ekona, for Buea, joining thousands of others who have had to rebuild their lives away from their roots. A well-wisher eventually helped her enroll in school in Buea.
Although the family sometimes visits their farm to collect food, it has not been possible to return permanently. Sidoine misses her former home and friends.

For younger children, displacement has also changed family routines. Twelve-year-old Michelle sells plantains while waiting for his mother to return from church. His 11-year-old cousin, Lorane, sometimes accompanies him. The two help their parents attract customers, particularly on weekends.
They also miss people they left behind in Ekona, including their grandmother, who died during a raid as a result of the crisis.

Susan Achuagoh, a mother of five whose house was burned during the conflict, has had to rebuild her livelihood as an orange seller in Buea. She gives her children small quantities of oranges to sell while she remains at her stall. This helps supplement their family income.
“I sell oranges; I give them small things to walk around with while I stay at the stall,” she shared in an interview with Global Voices. “If they do not help like that, it will not go at all.”

Her children’s education was interrupted for more than three years during the conflict. Another mother, Mami Blessing, says her children’s schooling was also disrupted and that they now help her at the market as the family struggles to make ends meet.

Godiva Ndang epse Limene, Education and Partnerships Officer at Street Child UK-Cameroon, says the prolonged crisis in the Northwest and Southwest has increasingly become a crisis of childhood, affecting education, protection, and development.

Children exposed to armed violence, displacement, and repeated insecurity may experience anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and social withdrawal. Taking on economic responsibilities can add to these pressures. Ndang says work that takes up time needed for learning, rest, and play can affect children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and physical development.

She stresses that helping in a family business is not automatically child labor. The distinction depends on the child’s age, the nature and duration of the activity, the risks involved, and whether it interferes with education, health, rest, or development.

The right to education is only one of the rights affected. Children also have a right to rest, leisure, and play, as well as protection from economic exploitation. For those uprooted from their communities, maintaining friendships, participating in cultural life, and developing a sense of belonging are also important parts of growing up.

The scale of the disruption remains significant. Figures from the Regional Delegations of Basic Education cited by UNICEF in September 2026 show that 223,749 children were completely out of school in the Northwest and Southwest, while 2,463 schools were non-operational. Of these, 2,005 were in the Northwest and 458 in the Southwest.

To educate children in conflict-affected communities, local partners including TeenAlive, the Foundation for Inclusive Education (FIED), Strategic Humanitarian Services (SHUMAS), and the Authentique Memorial Empowerment Foundation (AMEF) support Mobile Neighborhood Learning Corners and Satellite Learning Corners. These are established in accessible locations such as village chiefs’ homes, churches, schools, and community verandas.

The program has supported close to 100 learning corners across the two regions. Other education interventions include help with school enrollment, uniforms, and learning materials, as well as Teaching at the Right Level, a tutoring program.

Street Child also combines education with other forms of support. Its girls’ resilience and empowerment work provides displaced adolescent girls with life skills, literacy, and vocational training, alongside start-up kits and mental health assistance. Its Play for Peace initiative, supported by the FIFA Foundation, uses sports to promote peace, health, and education in conflict-affected communities.

Ndang says children also need psychosocial support, safe learning environments, and opportunities to play and interact with their peers. She adds that helping caregivers rebuild their livelihoods matters because reducing economic pressure on families can lessen the burden on children.

articles.title: 113th Grey Cup
paragraphs: The 113th Grey Cup was a Canadian football game played to decide the Canadian Football League (CFL) championship for the 2026 season. The game was played on November 15, 2026, at McMahon Stadium in Calgary, Alberta. It was the sixth time that Calgary hosted the Grey Cup, with the previous being in 2019. The West Division champion Edmonton Elks defeated the East Division champion Montreal Alouettes 37–30. This was their first Grey Cup win since 2015 and first since changing their team name in 2021.

In the regular season, the Elks finished first in their division with a 13–5 record. The Alouettes had finished with the best overall record in the league, 14–4, and were appearing in their third Grey Cup game in four years. These teams had previously met in the Grey Cup 11 times, of which Edmonton had won eight. Elks starting quarterback Cody Fajardo faced his former team, the Alouettes, who had traded him to Edmonton in 2024, after he was the Grey Cup MVP in 2023.

There were six lead changes during the game, tying a Grey Cup record. The Elks had seven scoring drives; the Alouettes kept pace until 1:42 remaining in the game, when they turned the ball over on downs. Edmonton then kicked a field goal to extend their lead to 37–27, effectively sealing the win. Fajardo was named the game's MVP, after throwing two passing touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns.

The game was televised in Canada nationally on CTV, TSN, Crave, and RDS. An average of four million viewers watched the game across these platforms, equalling the viewership figures from the previous year. The Canadian Forces Snowbirds made their final public flyover with the CT-114 Tutor during the national anthem.

The Edmonton Elks and Calgary Stampeders submitted bids in September 2024 to host the Grey Cup game in 2026. The Elks plan required renovation of their Commonwealth Stadium. The league announced in November 2024 that Calgary had been selected as host.

The same announcement set the date of the game as November 15, the earliest date that a Grey Cup championship game has been played. It was the fifth consecutive season that the Grey Cup was held on the third Sunday in November.

Before kickoff, a performance was given by Canadian singer-songwriters Jim Cuddy and Greg Keelor of Blue Rodeo, followed by the James Barker Band. The national anthem was sung by Canadian singer-songwriter Sarah McLachlan. This was followed by a flypast by the Snowbirds aerobatic team, in their final public display using the Canadair CT-114 Tutor aircraft. A half-time show featured American country singer Riley Green.

The game featured the Montreal Alouettes, playing in their 21st Grey Cup game, and their third in four years, facing the Edmonton Elks playing in their 24th Grey Cup match and their first since winning in 2015.

The Elks finished in first place in the West Division with a 13–5 record after finishing in fifth place with a 7–11 record the year prior, becoming the first team in league history to go from fifth place to first place in the division in the span of one season. After starting 0–2 for the previous five seasons, the Elks opened their season with three consecutive wins, including an overtime victory over the defending East Division champion Alouettes. The team was led in early in the year by the play of running back Justin Rankin, who was on pace for 1,000 yards both rushing and receiving after six games. The Elks started the season 6–1 before losing to the defending champion Saskatchewan Roughriders and the Alouettes in back-to-back weeks. The team later qualified for the playoffs for the first time since 2019 and for the first time since changing their team moniker to Elks following their victory over the Calgary Stampeders in the Labour Day Rematch. In Week 20, the Elks clinched first place in the West Division with a victory over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers which was their first Division title since 2015. The team finished with a 7–2 record in the last nine regular season games, including a loss in the final game of the season when the Elks were resting starters.

During the season, the Elks were led by CFL's Most Outstanding Player Finalist, Cody Fajardo, who finished with a career-high 4,788 passing yards and 25 passing yards in 17 starts along with 517 rushing yards and eight touchdowns. Rankin finished the season second in rushing with 1,170 yards and also had 640 receiving yards with ten scrimmage touchdowns. Placekicker Vincent Blanchard set a franchise record with 55 field goals and led the league in field goal accuracy with 93.2% while setting a single game record with nine field goals made in week 17's overtime victory over the Hamilton Tiger-Cats. The Elks led the West Division with nine players named as divisional all-stars.

In their first Division Final since 2019, the Elks hosted the BC Lions in their first playoff meeting since 2011. The first half was prominently a defensive battle as the teams exchanged field goals with the Lions leading 9–6 at the half. The Elks then owned the third quarter with ten points punctuated by Fajardo's 5-yard rushing touchdown near the end of the quarter. BC quickly responded with a Nathan Rourke rushing touchdown a couple of minutes later, tying the game at 16–16. The Elks then scored 12 unanswered points to secure the West Final victory by a score of 28–16, led by Fajardo who had 25 completions on 30 attempts for 274 yards and a passing touchdown with 84 rushing yards and a rushing touchdown.

The Alouettes finished in first place in the East Division with a 14–4 record and qualified for the playoffs for the seventh consecutive year. The team began the year with a 9–1 record with the only loss coming in overtime to the Edmonton Elks. In week 7, quarterback Davis Alexander broke Darian Durant's record for most consecutive pass attempts without an interception and finished with a 356-pass attempt streak before throwing his first pick. In a weak East Division, the Alouettes clinch a playoff berth and home playoff game after they defeated the BC Lions on Labour Day Weekend. team then clinched first place in the East in week 18 against the Winnipeg Blue Bombers in the same game where Tyson Philpot broke a franchise record for most receptions in a season. The Alouettes finished with a perfect record at home with their four losses occurring on the road.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI is a 2026 action-adventure game developed and published by Rockstar Games. It is the eighth main entry in the Grand Theft Auto series, following 2013's Grand Theft Auto V, and the sixteenth entry overall. Set in the fictional US state of Leonida, based on Florida, the story follows the criminal duo of Jason Duval (Dylan Rourke) and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez) as they lead a life of crime to escape from corrupt police officers in a state-wide criminal conspiracy. The game's open world allows players to freely roam Leonida and its Miami-inspired Vice City and engage in various side activities.

Preliminary work began in 2014 after the release of Grand Theft Auto V; principal production began after the 2018 launch of Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar's global development teams more than doubled since Red Dead Redemption 2. Miami and its surrounding areas were extensively researched for the game's world, which parodies Floridian and 2020s American culture. The protagonists' dynamic is inspired by Bonnie and Clyde, and the story was written to ensure players experience different areas of Leonida.

After years of speculation and anticipation, Rockstar confirmed in February 2022 that the game was in development. That September, footage from unfinished versions was leaked in what journalists described as one of the biggest leaks in the history of the video game industry. Grand Theft Auto VI was formally revealed in December 2023. After two delays, further leaks, and an extensive marketing campaign, it was released on 19 November 2026 for the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

Upon release, Grand Theft Auto VI was met with universal critical acclaim and achieved multiple records. The game sold 32.5 million copies before its release, becoming the most preordered video game of all time and one of the best-selling video games. Day-one retail sales reached $3.79 billion, making it the biggest entertainment launch in history. It is the only game from the 21st century to achieve an overall score of 99 on Metacritic among critics, tying with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998) as the highest-rated video game on the platform.

Grand Theft Auto VI is a single-player action-adventure game set within an open world and played from a third-person view as either Jason Duval or Lucia Caminos. Players can choose to fight non-player characters (NPCs), steal vehicles, rob establishments or get into high-speed chases with the police. When roaming freely, players have various options for activities, such as skydiving, wrestling, basketball, exercising, kayaking, and scuba diving.

Throughout the game, players can gain or lose weight—a returning feature from Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas—and if the player stays awake as either character for days on end, it will become visible on their faces. The "Criminal Profile" rating system tracks each player character's reputation based on their actions, similar to the honour system in Red Dead Redemption 2. This system evaluates the level of violence and escalation used during crime, dynamically altering in-game consequences and NPC reactions based on each character's reputation.

In free roam, as Jason or Lucia, players can choose to split up or do activities together. Their relationship, or lack of one, depends on the player's actions. Grand Theft Auto VI has an in-game social media app called Snapmatic, returning from Grand Theft Auto V. The app is meant to parody 2020s social media trends and apps, such as TikTok and Instagram. Players may customise the appearance of Jason and Lucia, changing their hair, clothes, and accessories.

The game has multiple endings. Upon completing the main storyline and viewing the end credits, the game reverts the narrative state to the moment before the final point-of-no-return prompt. In this post-game sequence, Jason and Lucia opt to postpone the confrontation and return to Vice City. Because the timeline resets before the climax, the final mission marker remains active on the in-game map, allowing players to continue free-roam exploration and re-initiate the finale at their discretion to achieve alternative endings. However, aside from replaying the finale, the game does not include a standard mission replay feature for earlier story chapters.

Grand Theft Auto VI is set in the fictional US state of Leonida, based on Florida. Its map is reported to be three times larger than the playable area of Red Dead Redemption 2. Leonida contains five counties: Vice-Dale County, Kelly County, Mariana County, Leonard County, and Lummox County. Notable locales featured are Vice City, the Grassrivers, and the Leonida Keys (inspired by Miami, the Everglades, and the Florida Keys, respectively). Other locations include Ambrosia, Mount Kalaga National Park, and Port Gellhorn. The game world parodies 2020s American culture, with satirical depictions of social media and influencer culture, law-enforcement tactics and technology like police body cameras, and references to Internet memes such as Florida Man.

The story follows a criminal couple: Jason Duval (Dylan Rourke), who worked for local drug runners in the Leonida Keys after serving in the US Army, and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez), the series' first canon female protagonist. After a failed score, the duo encounters a state-wide conspiracy and are forced to protect each other.

Other characters include Cal Hampton (Bobby Moynihan), Jason's paranoid friend; Boobie Ike (Mike Forbs), who runs a business empire in Vice City; Dre'Quan Priest (Naiqui Macabroad), owner of the record label Only Raw Records with Boobie; Bae-Luxe (Hood Brat) and Roxy (Krissy Celess), a musical duo signed to Only Raw under the name Real Dimez; Raul Bautista (Manny Pérez), a seasoned bank robber; Brian Heder (Stephen Root), a long-time drug runner in the Keys and Jason's landlord; and Mia Caminos (Roselyn Sánchez), Lucia's mother. Niko Bellic, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto IV, appears briefly in the game's later missions, with original performance capture actor Michael Hollick reprising his role.

articles.title: Jensen Huang
paragraphs: Jen-Hsun "Jensen" Huang (born February 17, 1963) is a Taiwanese and American electrical engineer and businessman. He co-founded the technology company Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable corporations, and served as its president and CEO from its founding in 1993 until his resignation in 2026. As of November 2026, Forbes estimates his net worth at US$110.1 billion, making him the 18th-wealthiest person in the world.

Born in Taipei, Huang spent his childhood in Taiwan and Thailand before immigrating to the United States. After earning a master's degree from Stanford University, he launched Nvidia alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem from a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California, in 1993. Huang led the company out of near-bankruptcy during the 1990s and oversaw its expansion from graphics processing unit (GPU) development into high-performance computing and artificial intelligence (AI).

Under Huang's leadership, Nvidia experienced massive growth during the AI boom, becoming the first company to reach a market capitalization of more than $5 trillion in October 2025. In 2021 and 2024, Time magazine included him in its list of the most influential people, and later named him as one of the "Architects of AI" for its 2025 Person of the Year. He was also awarded the IEEE Medal of Honor and the National Medal of Science in 2026 for his contributions to machine learning and computational science.

In November 2026, it was reported that Huang had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese business executive Alice Huang. The U.S. government initially suspected that she may have been a spy for China; later reporting disputed that there was conclusive evidence of this. As a result, Huang resigned from his positions at Nvidia, and the company confirmed that he would have no formal role at the firm going forward.

Huang was born in Taipei, Taiwan, on February 17, 1963, and moved to the southern city of Tainan as a child. He is the second son of Huang Hsing-tai, a chemical engineer at an oil refinery, and Lo Tsai-hsiu, a schoolteacher. They were a middle-class Taiwanese family that relocated often, and were native speakers of Taiwanese Hokkien. Each day, Jensen's mother randomly selected 10 words from the dictionary to teach her sons English. When he was five years old, Huang's family moved to Thailand to support his father's refinery career and remained there for approximately four years. He attended Ruamrudee International School while in Bangkok.

In the late 1960s, Hsing-tai traveled from Taiwan to New York City to train under an air conditioning company and, after returning home, resolved to send his sons to the United States. When he was nine years old, Jensen's parents sent him to live in the United States, even though he did not yet speak English fluently. He and his older brother moved in 1973 to live with an uncle in Tacoma, Washington. Both Huang's aunt and uncle were recent immigrants to Washington state; they accidentally enrolled him and his brother in the Oneida Baptist Institute, a religious reform academy in Oneida, Kentucky, for troubled youth, mistakenly believing it to be a prestigious boarding school. In order to afford the academy's tuition, Jensen's parents sold nearly all their possessions.

At the age of 10, Huang lived with his older brother in the boys' dormitory at Oneida Institute. Because he was too young to attend classes there, Huang enrolled at Oneida Elementary School, a public school in town, arriving as "an undersized Asian immigrant with long hair and heavily accented English". He was frequently bullied and beaten by classmates. In Oneida, Huang cleaned toilets every day, learned to play table tennis, joined a swimming team, and appeared in Sports Illustrated at age 14. He taught his roommate how to read in exchange for being taught how to bench press. In 2002, Huang said he remembered the part of his life in Kentucky "more vividly than just about any other".

Two years after Huang arrived in Oneida, his parents moved to the United States and settled in Beaverton, Oregon, after which the brothers withdrew from school in Kentucky to live with them. As a teenager, Huang attended Aloha High School in Aloha, Oregon, where he excelled academically. He skipped two grades, graduated at age 16, and became a nationally ranked table-tennis player, in addition to being a member of its mathematics, computer, and science clubs. In 1977, the school purchased an Apple II computer which Huang used to play Super Star Trek, a text-based video game, and to program in BASIC, creating his own version of Snake.

At the age of 15, Huang's first job was working the graveyard shift at a local Denny's restaurant as a dishwasher, busboy, and waiter from 1978 to 1983. After high school, he enrolled at Oregon State University because of its engineering program and affordable in-state tuition. He studied electrical engineering and graduated in 1984 with a bachelor's degree with highest honors. Huang later recalled, "I was the youngest kid in school, in class" and the only student who "looked like a child". While working as a microchip designer in Silicon Valley, he took graduate classes at Stanford University, where he earned a master's degree in electrical engineering in 1992.

After college, Huang worked as a microchip designer in Silicon Valley. He was approached for positions at Texas Instruments, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), and LSI Logic, ultimately choosing the California-based AMD due to already being familiar with the company. From 1984 to 1985, Huang designed AMD microprocessors while simultaneously attending Stanford and raising his two children. However, when he heard of new chip design processes at LSI Logic, Huang left AMD to assume a role as a technical officer at LSI Logic, working under a startup company, Sun Microsystems, where he met engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

LSI was in contract with Sun Microsystems and had introduced Huang to Malachowsky and Priem, who were working on a new graphics accelerator card. While the three produced the card's manufacturing process, the relationship between Malachowsky and Priem became strained as the two disputed the chip's design, leading to infighting; according to Malachowsky, they "broke every tool that LSI Logic had in their standard portfolio".

In 1989, Huang, Malachowsky, and Priem finalized the accelerator, which they called the "GX graphics engine". GX was a widespread financial success; the sales of the graphics engine contributed to Sun Microsystems' revenue increasing from $262 million in 1987 to $656 million in 1990, and Huang was promoted to be the director of LSI's CoreWare, a division that manufactured chips for hardware vendors. He stayed at LSI until 1993.

articles.title: Voyager 1
paragraphs: Voyager 1 is a space probe launched by NASA on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program, to study the outer Solar System and the interstellar space beyond the Sun's heliosphere. At a distance of 173.02 AU (25.9 billion km; 16.1 billion mi) as of November 2026, it is the most distant human-made object from Earth.

It was launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2. It communicates through the NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) to receive routine commands and to transmit data to Earth. Real-time distance and velocity data are provided by NASA and JPL.

The probe made flybys of Jupiter, Saturn, and Saturn's largest moon, Titan. NASA had a choice of either conducting a Pluto or Titan flyby. Exploration of Titan took priority because it was known to have a substantial atmosphere. Voyager 1 studied the weather, magnetic fields, and rings of the two gas giants and was the first probe to provide detailed images of their moons.

As part of the Voyager program and like its sister craft Voyager 2, the spacecraft's extended mission is to locate and study the regions and boundaries of the outer heliosphere and to begin exploring the interstellar medium. Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and entered interstellar space on August 25, 2012, making it the first spacecraft to do so. Two years later, Voyager 1 began experiencing a third wave of coronal mass ejections from the Sun that continued to at least December 15, 2014, further confirming that the probe is in interstellar space.

In 2017, the Voyager team successfully fired the spacecraft's trajectory correction maneuver (TCM) thrusters for the first time since 1980, enabling the mission to be extended by two to three years. Voyager 1 experienced successful revivals of several thrusters in 2018, 2019, and 2025.

Voyager 1's extended mission is expected to continue to return scientific data for several more years. As of 2026, two instruments are operational and returning data: the Plasma Wave Subsystem and magnetometer. Its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) may supply enough electric power to return engineering data until 2036.

A 1960s proposal for a Grand Tour to study the outer planets led NASA to begin work on a mission during the early 1970s. Initially, Voyager 1 was planned as Mariner 11 of the Mariner program. Due to budget cuts, the mission was reduced to a flyby of Jupiter and Saturn and renamed the Mariner Jupiter-Saturn probes. The name was changed to Voyager when the probe designs began to differ substantially from Mariner missions.

Voyager 1 was built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). It has a bus shaped like a decagonal (ten-sided) prism. It has 16 hydrazine thrusters, three-axis stabilization gyroscopes, and referencing instruments to keep the probe's radio antenna pointed toward Earth. Collectively, these instruments are part of the Attitude and Articulation Control Subsystem (AACS), along with redundant units of most instruments and eight backup thrusters. The spacecraft also included 11 scientific instruments to study celestial objects such as planets as it travels through space.

The radio communication system of Voyager 1 was designed to be used up to and beyond the limits of the Solar System. It has a 3.7-meter (12 ft) diameter high-gain Cassegrain antenna to send and receive radio waves via the three Deep Space Network stations on the Earth. The spacecraft normally transmits data to Earth over Deep Space Network Channel 18, using a frequency of either 2.3 GHz or 8.4 GHz, while signals from Earth to Voyager are transmitted at 2.1 GHz.

When Voyager 1 is unable to communicate with the Earth, its digital tape recorder (DTR) can record about 64 megabytes of data for later transmission. As of 2026, signals from Voyager 1 take 24 hours to reach Earth.

Voyager 1 has three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) mounted on a boom. Each MHW-RTG contains 24 pressed plutonium-238 PuO2 oxide spheres. The RTGs generated about 470 W of electric power at the time of launch, with the remainder being dissipated as waste heat. The power output of the RTGs declines over time due to the 87.7-year half-life of the fuel and degradation of the thermocouples. According to current plans, they may continue operating with at least one science instrument into the 2030s.

Unlike Voyager's other instruments, the operation of the cameras for visible light is not autonomous, but is controlled by an imaging parameter table contained in one of the digital computers, the Flight Data Subsystem (FDS). Since the 1990s, most space probes have been equipped with completely autonomous cameras.

The computer command subsystem (CCS) controls the cameras. The CCS contains fixed computer programs, such as command decoding, fault-detection and fault-correction routines, antenna pointing routines, and spacecraft sequencing routines. This computer is an improved version of the one that was used in the 1970s Viking orbiters.

The Attitude and Articulation Control Subsystem (AACS) controls the spacecraft orientation. It keeps the high-gain antenna pointing towards Earth, controls attitude changes, and points the scan platform. The custom-built AACS systems on both Voyagers are the same.

The Voyager 1 probe was launched on September 5, 1977, from Launch Complex 41 at the Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, aboard a Titan IIIE launch vehicle. The Voyager 2 probe had been launched two weeks earlier, on August 20, 1977. Voyager 1 reached both Jupiter and Saturn sooner, following a shorter trajectory.

Voyager 1's launch almost failed because Titan's LR-91 second stage shut down prematurely, leaving 1,200 pounds (540 kg) of propellant unburned. Recognizing the deficiency, the Centaur stage's onboard computers ordered a burn far longer than planned to compensate. Centaur extended its own burn and was able to give Voyager 1 the additional velocity it needed.

At cutoff, the Centaur was only 3.4 seconds from propellant exhaustion. If the same failure had occurred during Voyager 2's launch a few weeks earlier, the Centaur would have run out of propellant before the probe reached the correct trajectory. Jupiter was in a more favorable position vis-à-vis Earth during the launch of Voyager 1 than during the launch of Voyager 2.

Voyager 1's initial orbit had an aphelion of 8.9 AU (830 million mi), just a little short of Saturn's orbit of 9.5 AU (880 million mi). Voyager 2's initial orbit had an aphelion of 6.2 AU (580 million mi), well short of Saturn's orbit.

articles.title: Why AI-enabled scientific research is a double-edged sword
paragraphs: OpenAI has sparked a backlash in the mathematics community by apparently using AI to solve more than 700 longstanding maths problems in a short space of time. A recent open letter signed by 28 recipients of the Fields Medal (one of the highest honours in maths) goes some way to explaining why.

Mathematicians who have gone through some of the solutions offered by AI say they are opaque in their reasoning . As the open letter explains: “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

As famed mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao put it : “These companies are dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our communal village table and saying: ‘Here you go, I solved your food problem.‘”
OpenAI said it had consulted with the community prior to announcing the latest three results, one of which was in my own field of computer science .

Nevertheless, mathematicians are having to adapt fast to the disruptive arrival of AI in their field. This challenge extends far beyond mathematics and into all other disciplines of science and research.
The impact AI has had on software development through tools such as Claude and Codex, is undeniable. Industry software teams are now routinely using AI tools in their work.

But now, AI is already having a major impact on the practice of science itself. Academic journals and conferences are dealing with exponential increases in submissions from researchers, in a system largely based on volunteer effort for reviewing and editing.

This year, the International Conference on Learning Representations, a leading academic meeting on AI, received 60,000 submissions . This has increased from 490 in 2017. One researcher, commenting on the figures, said : “AI is breaking traditional academic peer review.”

This doesn’t seem to be a special case. In 2024, Mark A Hanson, from the University of Exeter, and colleagues, published a paper titled: “The strain on scientific publishing”. In it, the authors note that the total number of available academic articles has grown exponentially in recent years.

This is in part the result of a decades-long trend, predating modern generative AI, with many factors playing a role – including pressure on researchers to publish large numbers of academic articles, known as “publish or perish”. In 2022, just before ChatGPT launched, the number of papers published was about 47% higher than in 2016. The increase has occurred while the number of practising scientists has seen little growth. But AI is undoubtedly accelerating the process.

Yet this raises questions about whether the current trajectory is sustainable – and whether the quality of science will suffer. One academic conference has been testing whether AI could be part of the solution as well as the problem. This year, the NeurIPS meeting, which focuses on AI and machine learning, introduced a voluntary AI-assisted review for those submitting conference abstracts.
Afterwards, scientists evaluated the quality of the review and how helpful it was. But some in the field believe this could compound current problems.

Anecdotal evidence suggests some members of the public who are not professional scientists are using AI to produce and submit their own academic papers and write books on science. Citizen scientists make valuable contributions in areas such as biodiversity monitoring and astronomy.

But AI should not be viewed as a substitute for the formal training, daily research work, critical thinking and expert input from colleagues that academia offers. While AI and related technologies are powerful tools for democratising knowledge, it took me 13 years from my PhD to write my first book (the only one I have written so far), whereas now the same can apparently be done in weeks. But, as with peer review and maths proofs, humans have to check and interpret these.
As this story plays through and repeats, we may need to resort to new modes of scientific dissemination to deal with the new methods of creating research.

This brings me to the critical thinking that research requires. Currently, I provide the ideas, but increasingly rely on my AI assistant to do a lot of the work of thinking for me, or at least appear to. But the results of AI-enabled research can be obtuse, as the Terence Tao quote above illustrates, or even plain wrong. They can only be sorted out with human time and domain expertise.

I increasingly wonder what this means for the role of the researcher and for training the future generation of scientists, mathematicians and engineers. I am finding that a challenging, long term student project that would normally take several months to complete is at risk of being able to be almost completely automated through providing judicious prompts to an AI agent.

If I am guiding the student while they provide the prompts to an AI system, what do they learn from the process? And in my own research, where AI enables me to undertake projects I would not otherwise have the resources to, if I am providing the ideas but the AI is doing a lot of the “thinking” for me, am I even doing my own research anymore?
This could have an impact on the future generation’s ability to generate novel research questions, as well as their capacity for critiquing AI’s attempts to answer them.

One of my favourite sci-fi short stories is Profession, by Isaac Asimov. In it, the author imagines a future where young adults are educated by direct upload into their brains using technology known as magnetic tapes – which could be seen as a stand-in for AI. At one point, the main protagonist, George, tries to convince another character that humans can learn in other ways – by reading books, for example.

The other person is baffled, seeing this only as an unnecessary expense. Through the narrative, Asimov reveals the risks in the “direct upload” approach to learning. He also explores what is needed for society to progress when some forms of knowledge can be gained so easily.

We seem to be arriving at the science fiction future I once looked forward to where, like a science officer on a starship exploring unknown corners of the universe, or a billionaire genius tech superhero, I can just provide the ideas while getting the computer to do the heavy lifting. Like others, I am exhilarated by this, but also concerned about what it means for the practice and future of my discipline.

articles.title: AI helps uncover critical flaw in ubiquitous internet software
paragraphs: If you checked your bank balance, booked a flight or ordered groceries online today, there is a good chance your request was handled by a computer program written in Java.

For nearly three decades, the Java programming language has been one of the quiet workhorses of the internet. While most people rarely interact with it directly on their phones or laptops, it sits at the heart of most large, behind-the-scenes server applications that power modern business, finance and government.

That ubiquity is why a new critical security alert from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency drew the attention of technology teams worldwide. Security researchers uncovered a severe flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, in a core Java component. If left unpatched, the bug could allow an attacker to trick a vulnerable server into executing malicious code.

As a cybersecurity researcher who studies how large-scale software systems fail and how to defend them, I see this discovery as both a standard call to action for system administrators and another milestone in a broader shift: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how hidden flaws in critical software are discovered.
To understand the vulnerability, it helps to know why Java became so popular in the first place.

Normally, software must be tailored to the specific computer hardware and operating system it runs on. Java solved that headache with a clever piece of software called the Java Virtual Machine . It is essentially a program that runs other programs. Software developers write their Java application once, and the Java Virtual Machine provides a uniform foundation on top of a server’s operating system, running that application regardless of the underlying machine.

In addition to running the application, the Java Virtual Machine provides a standardized set of code for everyday tasks, such as reading files, managing network connections and formatting incoming data.

One of those routine tasks is Base64 encoding . Computers often need to send complex data, such as images, attachments or authentication tokens, over text-based internet protocols. Because raw binary data can be corrupted in transit, systems convert it into a string of standard text characters using Base64. When a Java server receives that string, its Base64 library decodes it back into its original form so the application can use it.

The newly discovered vulnerability resides in the Base64 decoding library in Oracle’s implementation of the Java Virtual Machine. This means that any application using this version of the Java Virtual Machine is at risk.

According to technical analysis of the flaw, a carefully crafted piece of malformed Base64 data can overwhelm the library’s processing, allowing an attacker to break out of normal boundaries, execute unauthorized commands and potentially gain control of the server.

If this sounds familiar, it follows a pattern seen recently with a high-profile PHP vulnerability, another foundational web language. Like the PHP vulnerability, this Java flaw was uncovered by cybersecurity firm Calif using AI tools to search for vulnerabilities.

Calif officials said the company alerted the governments of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain, and major tech companies, including Google and Microsoft, before the Java vulnerability became public. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency then issued its alert, urging organizations to immediately patch the flaw .

Historically, identifying subtle memory or parsing errors buried deep within millions of lines of mature code required months of painstaking manual review by human experts. Today, security researchers are pairing AI tools with traditional code analysis to systematically probe software libraries for edge cases that humans might overlook for years.
Whenever a critical vulnerability affects a foundational piece of software, headlines can sound alarmist. In reality, there are several reasons to maintain perspective while still acting quickly.

First, the good news is that a responsible security researcher discovered and privately reported this flaw, giving people who maintain software time to develop and release a fix before attackers could widely exploit it.
Second, everyday users do not need to panic about their personal devices. This is an issue affecting enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure, not home laptops, smartphones or tablets.

Third, even on vulnerable servers, exploiting this bug in the real world is not always straightforward. Most modern web systems do not expose raw Java decoders directly to the open internet. Instead, incoming traffic typically passes through several types of software – firewalls, load balancers and web proxies – that inspect, sanitize or reject malformed data before it reaches the underlying Java application.

Still, “harder to exploit” does not mean impossible, especially for internal systems or custom applications that pass user-supplied bits of information, called tokens, directly to Java’s decoder. As with any foundational infrastructure repair, the best defense is straightforward: promptly applying the latest security updates.
As AI accelerates the discovery of long-hidden software flaws, keeping the digital infrastructure patched remains one of the most effective cybersecurity practices.

articles.title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
paragraphs: Even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific. On November 15, 2026, the Fiji Meteorological Service began issuing updates about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands. Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades.

Named Xavier, the system intensified rapidly, thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones . Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only Wati, a short-lived storm that emerged in October.

As Xavier developed, NASA satellite data showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the El Niño that has been present in the region since June .

When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about 195 kilometers (120 miles) per hour. Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the cyclone intensity scale used in the region or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale .

The storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the international date line on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach . Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically shifts northeast during El Niño years. Research also shows that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an unusually rapid pace .

According to news reports, Xavier damaged homes and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands. It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa.

Xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months. A seasonal outlook from the Fiji Meteorological Service projects that the region could see between 11 and 15 named tropical cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the international date line. Storm activity in the Southwest Pacific basin typically peaks in February .

articles.title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
paragraphs: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.
This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit.

Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something.

CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization.
But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions, it’s even more difficult.

One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows.

One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.

Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well.
In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it.

In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks .

Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.
My research has found that risk to be high.

When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first.

Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.

Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.

In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?
Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake.

CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.

Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.

It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.

For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.

articles.title: Six-Day War
paragraphs: The Six-Day War, or the 1967 Arab–Israeli war (5–10 June 1967), was fought between Israel and a coalition of six Arab states, primarily Egypt, Syria, and Jordan, in the context of the Arab–Israeli conflict. The war, in which Israel conquered and occupied the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank of the Jordan River, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, shaped the political and strategic landscape of the Middle East into the 21st century. Many of the war's consequences remain unresolved.

The war broke out amid continual armed border incidents as well as rising Pan-Arab Nationalism, which aimed to unite Arab nations around opposition to Israel. In April 1967, a border incident between Israel and Syria, led to an aerial engagement in which six Syrian jets were shot down. This led to false reports by the Soviet Union that Israel intended to launch a major ground attack upon Syria.

In mid May, Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser mobilized 100,000 Egyptian troops to the border with Israel and ordered the immediate withdrawal of all UN peacekeepers from the region. Eight days later, Nassar announced that the Straits of Tiran, Israel’s only access to the Red Sea, would be closed to Israeli vessels. Israel had already stated that closure of the straits would be considered an act of war.

On 26 May, Nassar explained that the blockade meant "confrontation with Israel (and) also meant that we were ready to enter a general war with Israel. The battle will be a general one and our basic objective will be to destroy Israel".

On 30 May, Egypt signed a defense pact with Jordan, a pact with Syria having been concluded the previous November. The following day, at Jordan's invitation, the Iraqi army began deploying troops and armored units in Jordan.

On 1 June, Israel formed a National Unity Government by widening its cabinet, and on 4 June the decision was made to go to war. The war began on 5 June 1967 with Operation Focus, an Israeli surprise attack consisting of a series of airstrikes against Egyptian airfields and other facilities as the UNEF was leaving the zone. Israel caught Egyptian forces by surprise and destroyed nearly all of Egypt's air force, giving Israel air supremacy.

Simultaneously, the Israeli military launched a ground offensive into Egypt's Sinai Peninsula and the Egyptian-occupied Gaza Strip. Jordan joined the offensive later that morning, with an attack on West Jerusalem. After some initial resistance, Nasser ordered an evacuation of the Sinai Peninsula; by the fourth day of the conflict, Israel had occupied the entire Sinai Peninsula. On the fifth day, Syria joined the war by shelling Israeli positions in the north. By Saturday, Israeli forces occupied the Golan, and stabilized a position overlooking the Damascus Plain.

Egypt and Jordan agreed to a ceasefire on 8 June, and Syria on 10 June, and it was signed with Israel on 11 June. The Six-Day War resulted in more than 15,000 Arab fatalities, and fewer than 1,000 Israeli. Alongside the combatant casualties were the deaths of 20 Israeli civilians killed in Arab forces air strikes on Jerusalem, 15 UN peacekeepers killed by Israeli strikes in the Sinai at the outset of the war, and 34 US personnel killed in the USS Liberty incident, in which Israeli air and naval forces mistakenly assaulted a United States Navy spy ship.
