articles.title: How a Pittsburgh-born umpire painted baseball history onto the ball itself
paragraphs: Baseballs are charismatic objects. It is no accident that the narrative spine of novelist Don DeLillo’s magnum opus of 20th-century American life, “Underworld,” involves the ownership of the baseball from the “shot heard ’round the world” – the ninth-inning home run New York Giants slugger Bobby Thomson hit to beat the Brooklyn Dodgers for the 1951 National League pennant. A lot of Americana has been projected onto the surface of a baseball.

But the surface of a baseball is not typically a canvas. The 26 or so square inches of area, created when two pieces of leather are connected with 108 red stitches, are awkward surfaces on which to draw. And most of the time, the only thing people want drawn on baseballs is a signature from an admired player.
But that’s not how George Sosnak saw them.

Born in Pittsburgh in 1924, Sosnak worked as a minor league umpire starting in his 30s, but he became better known as a self-taught artist over the subsequent four decades. Each baseball offered Sosnak at least four spaces to fill with images of players, team insignia or text recounting playing statistics or triumphs, all meticulously rendered in India ink.
An ongoing exhibit at the Westmoreland Museum of American Art features over 60 of the approximately 800 balls he finished painting in his lifetime – he began painting nearly 3,000 balls.

Sosnak’s creations are often colorful, depicting players in action, with facts about them or their games written alongside. Many of the baseballs function as miniature stories, a spherical, secular altarpiece that tells the story of a key game or season.
His “ Pittsburgh Pirates, 1978 ” ball features Harold “Pie” Traynor, Bill Mazeroski and Roberto Clemente .

Traynor and Clemente had both died in 1972, the year Mazeroski retired, and the three never played on a single team together. Depicting three of Sosnak’s most legendary hometown Pirates together created a kind of pantheon, with the timeless image of Clemente finishing his swing juxtaposed with the specific moment Mazeroski raised his hat while circling the bases after hitting the home run that won the 1960 World Series .

Sosnak’s scenes often involve these juxtapositions, using the raised seams and the uneven leather strips to both separate and connect moments for artistic effect. He even depicted something other than baseball itself on the balls, including other sports. But his main focus was on using the spherical leather canvas to memorialize the moments and people that mattered to Sosnak – and to fellow fans who commissioned the balls. He often used such detail – spectators in Forbes Field represented by tiny ink dashes – that magnifying glasses are required to fully appreciate the nuances.

Sosnak linked the American folk art tradition with the talismanic nature of an actual baseball. Unlike the case in most other professional sports, some fans come away from baseball games with balls as souvenirs — whether they were hit as home runs or foul balls, or just tossed into the crowd by players.

Baseballs are disposable – most balls last only a few pitches, so around 100 balls are used in every professional game – and yet they become treasured relics when caught. Sosnak’s painted balls combine these tensions: You can hold one in your hand, visualizing its past while touching the otherwise disposable object that was imparted meaning only through the triumph.

articles.title: Cairngorm Plateau disaster
paragraphs: The Cairngorm Plateau disaster, also known as the Feith Buidhe disaster, occurred in November 1971 when six fifteen-year-old students from Edinburgh's Ainslie Park High School and their two leaders embarked on a two-day navigational expedition in a remote area of the Cairngorms in the Scottish Highlands.

While the group was on the high plateau, the weather deteriorated and they decided to head for the Curran shelter, a rudimentary refuge, which they failed to reach. The group became stranded in the open for two nights in a blizzard. Five youths and the leader's assistant died of exposure. A sixth student and the group's leader survived the ordeal with severe hypothermia and frostbite. The disaster is regarded as Britain's worst mountaineering accident.

A fatal accident inquiry led to formal requirements being placed on leaders for school expeditions. After acrimony in political, mountaineering and police circles, the Curran shelter was demolished in 1975.

The Cairngorms are a mountainous region of Scotland that are named after the 1,245-metre (4,085 ft) Cairn Gorm Mountain, which overlooks Aviemore, the main town in the area. The central region is an area of high granite plateau at about 1,200 metres (3,900 ft) and is deeply dissected by long glacial valleys, which run roughly from north to south. Between two of the valleys, the Lairig Ghru and the Lairig an Laoigh, extends the Cairngorm Plateau of granite boulders and gravel where Cairn Gorm itself and the 1,309-metre (4,295 ft) Ben Macdui, the highest mountain in the Cairngorms and the second-highest in the British Isles, are the main summits. The edges of the plateaux are in places steep cliffs of granite and popular for skiing, rock climbing and ice climbing.

Their height, distances and severe and changeable weather make the Cairngorms the most challenging range for climbers in the United Kingdom. Snow can fall at any time during the year, and snow patches can persist all summer. For snow and ice climbing, the area is the most dependable in Britain.

The plateau has a subarctic climate and supports only sparse tundra vegetation. The shattered terrain is more like the high ground in the arctic regions of Canada or Norway than the European Alps or North American Rocky Mountains. The weather often deteriorates rapidly with elevation, even when there are moderate conditions 150 metres below the plateau, the top can be stormy or misty and there can be icy or powdery snow. Even when no snow is falling, the wind can whip up snow on the ground to produce whiteout conditions a few metres above the surface, and snowdrifts can build up rapidly in sheltered places. Gravel can be blown through the air, and walking can be impossible. Scottish mountaineer Adam Watson explained how gale conditions can be extremely challenging on the plateau and make it difficult, if not impossible, to walk, see beyond a few metres, breathe and communicate with other party members. On 20 March 1986, a wind speed of 173 mph (278 km/h) was measured at Cairngorm summit weather station.

The valleys between the individual plateaux were used as drove roads by cattle drovers, who built rough protective shelters for their arduous journeys. Even today, between the Pass of Drumochter and the Lecht there are no paved roads over the Speyside–Deeside watershed, and the passes are impossible, even for four-wheel-drive vehicles. The Lairig Ghru pass between Speyside and Deeside is about 19 miles (30 km) long and reaches its greatest height at Pools of Dee at 810 metres (2,660 ft), where the water may be frozen over even in midsummer. The route has a total ascent of about 670 metres (2,200 ft) between habitation at Coylumbridge in Speyside and Linn of Dee. Towards the end of the 19th century, as droving died out, deer stalking estates were flourishing and the shelters were developed into bothies to provide improved, though still primitive, accommodation for gamekeepers. In modern times, the bothies have been taken over by the Mountain Bothies Association for use by trekkers and climbers to provide shelter and rough sleeping accommodation.

Starting in 1960 an area in the Northern Corries between Aviemore and Cairn Gorm was developed for alpine skiing. A road was constructed to an elevation of 650 metres (2,130 ft) in Coire Cas where a ski centre was built and ski lifts and tows were installed, one going up to a new restaurant, the Ptarmigan, at 1,080 metres (3,540 ft). In good weather it was an easy walk to the Cairngorm Plateau.

After the Second World War, the Scottish Council for Physical Recreation established Glenmore Lodge, beside Loch Morlich, on the road between Aviemore and the ski centre. In 1959, it moved to a purpose-built centre nearby (later the Scottish Centre for Outdoor Training, which provides training for leadership in mountaineering), and staff were on the spot to help in mountaineering emergencies.

In the 1960s, a military group erected, without permission from the local authorities, the St Valery, El Alamein and Curran shelters on the Cairngorm Plateau. They could often become buried in snowdrifts but they attracted hikers and campers. The Curran shelter was of metal covered with boulders, had a floor area 4 by 2 metres (12 by 7 ft) and was beside Lochan Buidhe, the highest standing water in Britain. Predicting that it would attract inexperienced walkers, Adam Watson and the Mountain Rescue Committee of Scotland wrote to the Nature Conservancy to point out the danger of a shelter in that location, but nothing was done about the matter.

Mountain rescue in the central Cairngorms was then the responsibility of the Scottish North Eastern Counties Constabulary. The mountain rescue teams consisted entirely of unpaid civilian volunteers and were co-ordinated by the Mountain Rescue Committee of Scotland, with the Cairngorm Mountain Rescue Team (MRT) being the first to be called on for assistance on the Cairngorm Plateau. They, in turn, could request helicopter support from RAF Kinloss. The Braemar MRT and Kinloss RAF MRT would also attend if there was a major incident, or if the location for the rescue was uncertain.

articles.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
paragraphs: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U.S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1.3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon .

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc., selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.
NASA’s SBIR/STTR program is part of the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate and is managed by NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

articles.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother: the sacred and profane collide in this off-kilter hitman drama
paragraphs: A grieving widower with three children and a dwindling supply of frozen breast milk is an unlikely premise for a crime thriller. Yet this is where Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother begins, moving between the intimate demands of fatherhood and a criminal underworld populated by characters who might have stepped from the pages of a comic book.
Director Bassam Tariq’s latest film has moments of domestic tenderness sitting alongside brutal violence, with strange flashes of black humour emerging in the most unexpected places.

Mahershala Ali plays Latif, a devout Muslim and hitman struggling to raise his three children following the death of his wife. In their cramped Texas flat, teenage daughter Fatiha (Adia), eight-year-old Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) and baby Aziza are adjusting to life without their mother. Heartbreakingly, the supply of his late wife’s frozen breast milk is running out, and the baby cannot tolerate formula. This affecting detail highlights the mother’s absence in the daily routines of a household still dependent upon her.

Ali brings an effortless gravity to Latif. Physically imposing yet remarkably still, he conveys a man weighed down by guilt and the responsibilities of fatherhood. There is an economy to his movements which lends poignancy to even the smallest domestic encounters. His capacity for violence appears incongruous with this quiet presence, until he is drawn back into the work he knows.

Crime boss Mike (Laith Nakli) orders Latif to kill Pastor Hwan (John Cho), a former Marine leading a heavily armed group of Christian fundamentalists. Hwan has threatened Mike’s nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali), who runs a pornography and sex work operation. These figures are grotesque and absurd, verging on caricature, sometimes provoking uneasy laughter with their excesses.

At the heart of the film is Adia’s compelling performance as Fatiha. On the cusp of adulthood, she is beginning to test the boundaries of her independence, even as her mother’s absence places increasing demands upon her at home. The pull of a life beyond the family competes with the needs of her younger siblings. Adia’s emotional intensity gives these domestic tensions a rawness which feels entirely authentic.

The film frequently draws the sacred and profane together in provocative imagery. Latif’s Muslim faith is deeply held, shaping his daily rituals and sense of moral responsibility, though his work as a hired killer presents an uncomfortable contradiction.

His choice of a sword over a gun adds an almost surreal quality to the violence, particularly against the film’s contemporary setting. Pastor Hwan offers a more twisted, fanatical expression of religious belief, using his Christian fundamentalism to justify brutality.

Tariq had originally planned to work with Ali on Marvel’s Blade which was cancelled during development . Certainly, Ali’s acrobatic and inventive sword work in the fight scenes wouldn’t have looked out of place in Marvel’s scrapped vampire-slayer movie. These big fight scenes can jar when juxtaposed with tender moments, but Ali has the presence to pull it off with aplomb, creating an oddly unsettling atmosphere.

Tariq’s cinematography and soundtrack add to this disquiet. Inverted views of the city render familiar streets strange, while the soundtrack occasionally evokes religious chanting. These unexpected flourishes add to the film’s peculiar, off-kilter sensibility.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother occasionally feels uneven. The tonal shifts between domestic realism and outlandish violence are not always comfortably resolved. Tariq’s appetite for the grotesque sometimes threatens to overwhelm the more affecting family drama, though there is much to admire in the film’s refusal to shy away from its own peculiarities.

It is in the relationships between Latif and his children, and the bonds that hold them together in their mother’s absence, that the film finds its greatest strength. There is bloodshed and violence aplenty, but who would have thought the hardest thing to watch would be a little spilled breast milk.

articles.title: Mairzy Doates
paragraphs: Mairzy Doates (April 1, 1976 – May 25, 1998) was an American Thoroughbred racehorse and multiple graded stakes winner, most remembered for her victory at the inaugural Japan Cup in 1981. Owned by New York City art dealer Arno D. Schefler and trained primarily by future U.S. Racing Hall of Fame inductee Horatio Luro, she competed successfully across the United States from 1978 to 1981, including winning the Yerba Buena Handicap twice.

In her final race, she traveled to Tokyo to contest the first Japan Cup, an international invitational established by the Japan Racing Association (JRA) to assess Japanese horses' performance against the rest of the world. She defeated the field in a course-record time, which alongside the strength of the other foreign horses, was widely considered as evidence of the disparity between Japanese and international horse-racing standards. Her performance is frequently credited as the catalyst for the JRA's long-term initiative to improve the caliber of Japanese breeding and racing. Following her victory, which made her 1981's highest-earning mare globally, Mairzy Doates retired from racing to become a broodmare in Midway, Kentucky. She gave birth to nine foals before dying at the age of 22.

Mairzy Doates was born April 1, 1976, bred by Preston and Patrick Madden, a pair of horse-training brothers who operated out of Hamburg Place in Kentucky. Her sire was Nodouble, a multiple graded stakes winner who had retired to stud in 1970, and later became the leading sire in North America in 1981. In contrast, her dam, Avalanche Lily, had only raced lightly and never won, but she was a foal of leading sire and 1960 Grass Horse of the Year T. V. Lark, and a descendant of Man o' War. Mairzy Doates's mare line traces directly to Cinq a Sept, winner of the 1927 Irish Oaks, making Mairzy Doates a distant relative of Secretariat.

Two years later in 1978, Arno D. Schefler, a New York art dealer and investment banker who had dealt in Thoroughbred horses since 1967, purchased Mairzy Doates as a filly from the Maddens. Schefler was the one to name her, referencing the novelty song "Mairzy Doats" made popular in a 1943 recording by bandleader Al Trace. She was briefly trained by Angel Penna and then Mickey Preger, but by winter, Schefler had handed Mairzy Doates over to Horatio Luro, a veteran horse-trainer with whom Schefler had become acquainted in the early 1970s. Mairzy Doates was brought to Luro's stable in Miami, where she had to be closely monitored while training due to the weakness of her ankles.

Mairzy Doates raced once as a two-year-old, finishing sixth out of ten at the Aqueduct Racetrack on December 22, 1978. Over two months, Mairzy Doates vied several times for a maiden race victory, eventually winning on her fourth attempt on February 4, 1979. Her first graded race, the Grade 3 Ruthless Stakes on February 18, went poorly; Mairzy Doates remained thoroughly distanced from the other horses for the entirety of the race until her jockey eased her before the finish line. Nevertheless, Mairzy Doates continued to race throughout the rest of the year, winning several allowance races and placing third in the Grade 1 Alabama Stakes. By December, and at her final race of the year at the Busher Handicap, commentators had noted Mairzy Doates's improved performance.

The next year, Schefler wished to race Mairzy Doates on the West Coast due to more racing opportunities being available in the area. Luro suggested that Mike Whittingham, the son of the U.S. Racing Hall of Fame trainer Charlie Whittingham, take over as trainer during their Western campaign. Mairzy Doates did not manage to place higher than fifth in both of her next two graded races: the Grade 1 Santa Barbara Handicap on March 23 and the Grade 2 Gamely Handicap on May 4. However, on May 26, 1980, she achieved her first graded victory at the Golden Gate's Grade 3 Yerba Buena Handicap in dominant fashion, beating her opponents "about as easily as a horse can" in the 1+3⁄8 mi race by six lengths and with a winning time of 2:15.

In July, Mairzy Doates was announced as an entrant in the Grade 2 Matchmaker Stakes, a race so-called as the top three placers' owners were given the choice of several high-end stallions for stud services, but had to withdraw after suffering a high fever. Around this time, Mairzy Doates was injured and returned to train under Luro; she was not able to race again until December 22, where she won an allowance race by three lengths over Quick As Lightning.

In her final year of racing in 1981, Mairzy Doates again failed to win a Grade 1 race in her three attempts, her best performance being a narrow defeat by a nose in the Santa Barbara Handicap. In her following races, she subsequently achieved a triple run of graded victories. She repeated her previous win in the Yerba Buena Handicap with a similar large margin of victory, then edged out Love Sign in the Grade 3 New York Handicap. Finally, at the Matchmaker Stakes, she made up for her withdrawal from the previous year's race with a 1+1⁄4 length victory over Honey Fox. Schefler considered using his awarded choice of stallion to pair leading stallion Raja Baba with Mairzy Doates, although this plan ultimately fell through and Raja Baba was instead paired with another of Schefler's mares. By July, Mairzy Doates was considered a leading contender for turf-racing fillies in North America, and placed in her final two Grade 2 races in the year.

In November 1981, Mairzy Doates was one of several American horses invited to Tokyo to take part in the first running of the Japan Cup, an international race over 2,400m designed by the Japan Racing Association (JRA) to assess the performance of their horses against the rest of the world on home turf. While the JRA had attempted to invite several prominent horses such as John Henry, the final line-up of international horses was ultimately deemed unremarkable, while Japan fielded an "all star cast", including the year's autumn Tennō Shō's top three finishers. The most favored entrant of the international group was The Very One, the same horse to whom Mairzy Doates had lost that year's Santa Barbara Handicap by a nose. The Very One had previously run against Mairzy Doates on three other occasions, each time either winning or placing higher than her. While Mairzy Doates's team accepted the invitation, Luro, now 80 years old and recovering from pneumonia, sent John Fulton to cover as trainer.
